case_study_insert.main_stem: Amberfield Theme Park (ATP) is a public limited company in the leisure and attractions sector in the Midlands, employing a workforce of 130. Founded in 2004 by Priya Raval, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership to keep ride operations standardised and safe. ATP plans to invest $1,200,000 in a new roller coaster and water ride, financed by a $700,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $504,000 a year, a variable cost of $22 a unit and a selling price of $58, and produces 22,000 units a year in paid visitor admissions. ATP faces high seasonal labour turnover and rising complaints about queue times at peak weekends.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Peak Season 2025: ATP welcomed 6,400 visitors on peak days, with average queue time rising from 24 to 41 minutes. Complaints grew from 52 to 96 per week, and 57% of a 500-visitor survey cited queues. Ride downtime reached 3.6% of operating hours. 18 of 130 seasonal staff left within six months; external ride-operator training costs $780 per worker while induction coaching is in-house. Repeat-visit intention fell from 61% to 49%.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Amberfield Theme Park as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Attractions Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The base interest rate increased from 4.75% to 5.5%, lifting finance costs on the new loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.0% from $12.50 to $13.38 per hour from April 2026, affecting seasonal staff. (3) Electricity and maintenance input costs have risen 13.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on paid attractions grew 4.6%.

questions.question_text: ATP plans to fund part of its $1,200,000 ride expansion with a bank loan. Explain two advantages for ATP of using the $700,000 share issue instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Equity from the $700,000 share issue carries no interest or capital repayments, so ATP's cash flow is protected while it already meets fixed costs of $504,000 a year. Money not paid to a lender can be spent on reducing the 41-minute queues and the 3.6% ride downtime behind the 96 weekly complaints, protecting the $58 ticket price and the 22,000 admissions sold.

Point 2: A share issue lets a public limited company raise a large sum for the $1,200,000 roller coaster and water ride without pledging park assets as collateral, so the rides are not at risk of repossession if visitor numbers miss target. Unlike the $500,000 loan, equity needs no debt service in the early years when the new rides are bedding in. The cost is dilution of existing shareholders, but with autocratic leadership and a hierarchical structure, Priya Raval can still direct ride operations and safety while the extra capital funds growth.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue over a bank loan (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to ATP's $700,000 share issue, $1,200,000 expansion and cash flow.

questions.question_text: ATP wants to drive demand for its new rides. Consider a national television campaign, local radio advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should ATP choose to promote the new rides? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television campaign: A TV advert would build mass awareness of the roller coaster and water ride across the Midlands and beyond, potentially filling the extra capacity quickly. Production and airtime are very expensive, however, and much of the audience is too far away to visit, so wastage is high for a business already funding a $1,200,000 expansion with $504,000 fixed costs. TV also cannot easily show the 41-minute queue problem being solved.

Local radio advertising: Radio is cheap, reaches the immediate catchment that fills the 6,400 peak-day visits, and suits short-notice messages about new rides. Its reach is narrow, however, and cannot by itself attract the wider growth of 4.6% in spending on paid attractions, so it is best used for last-minute offers.

Social media influencer marketing: Theme-park and family influencers can show the new rides to exactly the visitor segment ATP needs, at low cost per booking and with measurable engagement. Content can address the 57% of surveyed visitors who complained about queues by highlighting improvements, and it can adapt quickly when 3.6% ride downtime changes conditions. Results build more slowly than TV and depend on credible influencers.

Recommendation: ATP should choose social media influencer marketing, with local radio for last-minute promotion. It reaches the growing attractions market cost-effectively and can repair the repeat-visit intention that fell to 49%; television is rejected as unaffordable and wasteful for a business already carrying a $500,000 loan, and radio is rejected as too narrow to fill a $1,200,000 ride expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States simple promotional ideas with little reference to ATP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ATP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of ATP's queues, complaints and expansion with a justified recommendation that rejects the alternatives.

questions.question_text: ATP has high seasonal labour turnover and rising complaints about queue times. Explain two benefits for ATP of its autocratic leadership style in addressing these problems.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Autocratic leadership allows Priya Raval to make fast decisions on ride staffing and queue management, so the 41-minute waits and 96 weekly complaints can be tackled at once during peak weekends. In a hierarchical structure, instructions flow quickly to the 130 staff, closing rides with 3.6% downtime and redeploying workers to queues, which protects the $58 admission price and the 22,000 visitors.

Point 2: Clear, top-down rules also keep ride operations standardised and safe while eighteen seasonal staff leave every six months. New workers receive unambiguous procedures, reducing accidents and inconsistency that could worsen the 57% of complaints about queues. Decisive control supports the $1,200,000 ride investment because safety and throughput can be enforced without waiting for committee agreement, protecting the $36 contribution per admission.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of autocratic leadership (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to ATP's queues, downtime, turnover and safety.

questions.question_text: ATP must reduce ride downtime and improve operator skills. Consider external ride-operator training at $780 per worker or in-house induction coaching. Which should ATP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
External ride-operator training: A $780 course gives formal, up-to-date safety and operating skills, which can help cut the 3.6% ride downtime and address the 57% of visitor complaints about queues caused by slow operations. For the 18 seasonal staff who left, replacing and training newcomers externally costs $14,040, affordable beside a $1,200,000 expansion. The downsides are that workers are off the rides during training, reducing peak capacity when 6,400 visitors arrive, and generic content may not cover ATP's exact rides.

In-house induction coaching: Senior operators can train new staff on the actual rides at no cash cost, keeping throughput high and teaching ATP's own procedures, which suits a hierarchical structure with standardised operations. It avoids the $14,040 spend and works with seasonal staff who leave quickly. However, it lacks a recognised certificate, uses senior staff time, and may repeat bad habits, which is risky when 96 weekly complaints already signal problems.

Decision: ATP should choose in-house coaching for routine induction, with external $780 courses for ride supervisors. Coaching is free, ride-specific and avoids removing staff at peak times when queues are already 41 minutes. Full external training is rejected because $14,040 and lost operating hours would hurt peak throughput, while coaching alone is rejected because it lacks formal safety certification.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two training methods with little reference to ATP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of ATP's costs and safety.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in the context of ATP with a justified decision covering certification, cost and peak capacity.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ATP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $504,000 ÷ ($58 − $22) = $504,000 ÷ $36 = 14,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 14,000 visitor admissions a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $58 − $22 = $36. Answer: contribution per unit is $36.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ATP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 14,000-unit break-even output with 22,000 admissions sold to confirm the park is profitable, giving a margin of safety of 8,000 admissions, which supports the $1,200,000 ride investment.
2. Use the $36 contribution to model a $4 off-peak ticket discount to $54: contribution falls to $32 and break-even rises to $504,000 ÷ $32 = 15,750 admissions, still below 22,000, so quieter days can be promoted.
3. Use fixed costs of $504,000 and $36 contribution to set the admission target needed to service the $500,000 loan on the new rides.
4. Benchmark unit cost ($504,000 ÷ 22,000 + $22 = $44.91 an admission) to detect waste behind 3.6% ride downtime and judge whether the $22 variable cost is rising with 13.4% electricity and maintenance inflation.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 14,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $36 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 8,000 against 22,000 admissions; off-peak discount modelling; loan-service target for the $500,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $44.91 to monitor downtime and energy costs.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate ATP's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has ATP's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.79 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.64 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.33 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.14 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $55,000 inventories + $70,000 trade receivables + $90,000 cash = $215,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $95,000 + $65,000 = $230,000. 2024 short-term cover = $215,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.79; 2025 = $230,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.64. The inventory-excluding measure for 2024 = ($215,000 − $55,000) ÷ $120,000 = $160,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.33; for 2025 = ($230,000 − $70,000) ÷ $140,000 = $160,000 ÷ $140,000 = 1.14.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. Cover of short-term obligations fell from 1.79 to 1.64 because current liabilities rose from $120,000 to $140,000 faster than current assets, which grew only from $215,000 to $230,000. Cash fell from $90,000 to $65,000 while trade receivables rose from $70,000 to $95,000, so more wealth is tied up in amounts owed. The inventory-excluding measure fell from 1.33 to 1.14, confirming the decline is not merely a stock effect. This is a concern while ATP is spending $1,200,000 on new rides and carrying a $500,000 loan.

Conclusion: ATP's financial position has not improved. Both the current ratio (1.79 to 1.64) and the acid test ratio (1.33 to 1.14) show weaker short-term solvency. The falling cash balance is the main risk, so ATP should tighten credit control and consider delaying some capital spending until liquidity recovers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of cash, receivables and liabilities and a justified conclusion on deterioration.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ATP of introducing paid fast-track queue lanes at peak times.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Fast-track lanes let ATP charge extra for skipping the 41-minute queues that drove 57% of complaints and the fall in repeat-visit intention to 49%. For a workforce of 130 and fixed costs of $504,000, the extra revenue adds to the $36 contribution per admission and helps service the $500,000 loan, while giving dissatisfied visitors a tangible improvement.

Disadvantage: Charging to jump queues can be seen as unfair by families who already paid $58, possibly worsening complaints from 96 a week and the 49% repeat-visit figure. Fast-track also does not add ride capacity; with 3.6% downtime and $780 training needs, it merely reorders the same queues, so underlying throughput problems remain and the $1,200,000 investment may still be underused.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to ATP's queues, complaints, price and capacity.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 7.0% minimum wage increase and the 13.4% rise in input costs will affect ATP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.5%): If ATP's $500,000 loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $500,000 = $3,750 a year (0.0075 × $500,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $504,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate there is no extra cost. Higher rates may also reduce family spending on days out, but ATP can largely remove the financing risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (7.0%, to $13.38 per hour): With a workforce of 130, many ride operators and seasonal staff are hourly paid, so the wage bill rises and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so a defensible annual total cannot be invented. The honest test is given productivity: 22,000 admissions ÷ 130 staff = about 169 admissions per worker, so the rise is bearable only if productivity holds or the new rides lift visitor numbers; otherwise the $36 contribution per admission falls.

Input cost inflation (13.4% in electricity and maintenance): The $22 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 13.4%, that adds 13.4% × $22 = $2.95 per admission, or about $64,900 a year at 22,000 admissions (22,000 × $2.95). Even a smaller rise would cut the $36 contribution materially, and it applies to every visitor while 3.6% downtime already signals maintenance costs.

Conclusion: The 13.4% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 22,000 admissions and directly erodes the $36 contribution needed to justify the $1,200,000 rides. The interest rise is only about $3,750 and can be fixed, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity of about 169 admissions per worker, whereas energy and maintenance inflation has no immediate offset.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies external changes with limited application to ATP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on ATP's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of ATP with a well-justified greatest-impact judgement and reasons for rejecting the other two.
